article_text:
As France marks the bicentennial of photography, Paris Photo considers the history and future of a constantly evolving medium

When was photography invented? France is drawing a line in the sand at 1827 when, between 04 June and 18 July, Nicéphore Niépce fixed an image of the view from a window in his country estate. The nation is celebrating the bicentennial from September 2026 to September 2027 and the first major event in the calendar is Paris Photo; the history and technology of image-making will thread through the fair. “Paris Photo presents a panorama of photography, from the 19th century to the latest experimentations with digital art. This year even more, we will highlight the diversity of photography practices through 200 years of history,” says Florence Bourgeois, director of Paris Photo. “There will be a focus on the historical thread of the medium.”

The fair will feature a retrospective by Thomas Ruff, a contemporary artist renown for his work investigating the nature and technology of photography; his installation will include works from Sterne (‘ Stars ’, 1989–1992), made with images from the European Southern Observatory, and from Jpegs (2004–2009), pixelated images of landscapes, modern technology and historical events. Florian Ebner and Damarice Amao, from the Centre Pompidou/Musée National d’Art Moderne, have been invited to curate a show on the development of photography, meanwhile, drawing on the institution’s collection with Julie Jones, director of the Maison Européenne de la Photographie. And the booths will include more galleries presenting prints from the early years of image-making.

“We look at the history of photography from a contemporary point of view,” explains Anna Planas, artistic director of Paris Photo. “To mark the bicentenary, our entrance statement will be dedicated to the work of Thomas Ruff, across a wall of nearly 40 meters long at the entrance of the Grand Palais. The installation will highlight Ruff’s engagement with the medium and its evolving technologies offering an exploration of the grammar of photography.”

“This year we will welcome galleries and publishers from 38 countries – the fair is becoming more and more open” – Anna Planas

Other presentations will also consider photography as a medium. Galerie Christophe Gaillard is bringing a solo display by Isabelle Le Minh, for example, a contemporary artist who highlights the new properties of digital images; London’s Large Glass “will confront historical work with contemporary in a show where each artist is paired with a historical figure, connected by places of significance or shared themes,” says Planas. The Voices sector, which is curated by Francesco Zanot and Zasha Colah and dedicated to contemporary image-makers, will explore an emerging paradox – conceived as a tool to preserve that which would otherwise vanish, photography is being celebrated just as its traditional form appears unstable, transformed and challenged by processes altering its nature and status.

Titled La Disparition (‘ The Disappearance ’), Voices will include work by Léonard Pongo, a Belgian-Congolese artist who plays with the limits of visibility. Pongo’s work was presented in the 2026 Venice Biennale and, says Planas, the 2026 Voices curators bring insight into both photography and the contemporary art landscape. “Francesco is a photography curator and researcher,” she explains. “Zasha comes from the contemporary art world. This is something we also really enjoy, opening up to curators from outside photography.”

The Digital sector will be curated by Marco De Mutiis, digital curator at Fotomuseum Winterthur in Switzerland, and editor of the 2025 publication The Lure of the Image . Bringing the medium up to the present day, his selection also draws on a longer history of photography and of digital imaging. “Photography has been a continuously unstable, constantly changing medium,” he says. “And digital has fundamentally transformed it. But there is also a specificity of the image that has formed how we see the world. The Digital sector will include artists who show how photography has changed, from glitches and Photoshop to AI and machine learning, but we will also consider that ongoing history.”

Photography’s roots are in science, positivism and the drive for efficiency, he adds, “and we should always remember that the camera was invented in the time of the Industrial Revolution, a time of an ideology which was powerful in erasing other forms, and which still lies at the root of many neoliberal societies”. But there is also an alternative history of photographs linked with spiritualism, ghosts and the occult, he argues, more esoteric beliefs which are somehow resurfacing now.

“I have been interested to see many artists now coming back to magic, perhaps as a way to escape the algorithm,” he says. “This algorithm seems to be dictating our lives, so forms that are subjective or embrace mystery and even magic are an escape from that, almost a refuge or resistance to this scientific eye.”

Elsewhere at Paris Photo other alternative histories will also be traced. An association of Argentinian galleries will show how photography developed in the country, for example, with Rolf Art presenting innovative artist Adriana Lestido, and Vasari bringing a group show – after last year devoting its booth to Julio Le Parc, the groundbreaking op artist now showing a major retrospective at Tate Modern.

The Emergence sector will include Randa Mirza, who photographs the south of Lebanon, and shows the destruction caused by Israeli attacks; it will also feature Nicolás Combarro, whose work considers concentration camps and how to depict them, in the absence of historical images. Over in the talks programme, Tina Campt, professor of humanities at Princeton University and author of books such as Listening to Images , and A Black Gaze: Artists Changing How We See, will be in-conversation with South African visual activist and photographer Zanele Muholi.

“We trigger as much diversity as possible,” says Planas. “This year we will welcome galleries and publishers from 38 countries – the fair is becoming more and more open, and the bicentenary may also have an attractive effect to the international community.”

“Through our conversation and book talks programmes, curated paths and specific presentations, we have the will to give a wide vision of photography today,” adds Bourgeois.

Paris Photo takes place from 12-15 November 2026 at the Grand Palais.

article_text:
Taiwan is getting a dedicated national focus at the International Classic Film Market ( MIFC ), the industry arm of Lyon’s Lumière Festival, the first for a non-European country, according to the Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute (TFAI).

A new 4K restoration of Chen Kun-hou’s “ Osmanthus Alley ” leads the Taiwan in Focus program, which runs alongside this year’s guest country, Greece.

Related Stories

Belgian Series 'The Inheritance' Scores Sony Pictures Television Award at Rome’s MIA Market

Sony Pictures Television Hires Lauren Glaubach, Former YouTube and Pinterest Exec, to Lead Digital and Social Distribution Strategy

TFAI is using the showcase to seek international distribution and programming partners for the island’s restored classics. “Osmanthus Alley” made its world premiere at the festival on Oct. 12, with Chen and star Lu Hsiao-fen in attendance. TFAI says distributors it has previously worked with have expressed interest, with release terms and timing still under negotiation.

Adapted from Hsiao Li-hung’s novel, the film follows Thik-hông (Lu), an orphan who marries into a wealthy family, is widowed young and sees her son sent away to Japan, leaving her isolated behind the walls of the family estate. Simon Yam and Tuo Tsung-hua appear in guest roles. Lu won best actress at the 1987 Asia Pacific Film Festival, and the theme song, with lyrics by Wu Nien-jen, took the Golden Horse for best original film song.

The restoration also brings back the film’s original Taiwanese soundtrack. Chen insisted on shooting in Taiwanese, but state-run Central Motion Picture Corporation (CMPC) chose to release the film in Mandarin, in line with the government’s policy of promoting the language at the time. Chen eventually persuaded the studio to produce a Taiwanese version, but it played in only a limited number of theaters and gradually faded from view.

Its selection coincides with the 70th anniversary of Taiwanese-language cinema, which TFAI traces to 1956’s “Xue Pinggui yu Wang Baochuan.” An estimated 1,200 Taiwanese-language films were made between the 1960s and 1981, but only about 200 survive in TFAI’s collection. The restoration also anticipates TFAI’s 2027 focus on literary adaptations, while Chen’s lifetime achievement award at the 2023 Golden Horse Awards prompted renewed interest in his work.

Chen began as a cinematographer, winning a Golden Horse for “He Never Gives Up” (1978), and from 1979 worked closely with Hou Hsiao-hsien, the pair often trading roles behind the camera. Chen’s “Growing Up” won him the Golden Horse for best director in 1983.

TFAI restored “Osmanthus Alley” from its original 35mm negative, filling missing frames from an interpositive, with audio drawn from the 35mm Taiwanese sound negative. The source was generally in good condition, but mold spots and dense clusters of small white specks required careful treatment. Aggressive cleaning settings risked erasing image detail, so technicians used masks and adjusted processing settings before completing frame-by-frame manual repairs.

In line with FIAF’s code of ethics, Chen was repeatedly consulted. An intermediate version had more saturated, vibrant colors, but discussions with the director led to a more subdued final grade, closer to the original photography.

Tu Duu-chih, who handled the film’s original sound mix, returned to help restore the Taiwanese soundtrack from six primary audio reels. The team synchronized the material, repaired damaged sections and reduced noise through multiple passes using light processing settings.

The soundtrack holds another connection to Taiwanese cinema history. Cast members who did not speak Taiwanese were dubbed in post-production: co-star Lin Hsiu-ling voiced Lu’s dialogue, while Hou provided the voice for Tuo.

TFAI, which holds about 20,000 film titles, restores 10 to 12 films a year and has restored more than 100 since 2013. Physical deterioration prompts climate control and emergency digitization, but a full restoration depends on whether a film has “a clear purpose and an audience ready to experience it right now,” the institute says. Recent restorations include Tsai Ming-liang’s “Vive L’Amour,” which screened in Venice Classics in 2025, and “The Dull Ice Flower,” chosen by Taiwanese audiences in a public poll and selected for Cannes Classics this year. Taiwanese-language titles “Love Never Ceases” and “Zhang Di Seeks A-Zu” were restored for the anniversary.

Overseas, TFAI prioritizes in-person screenings to introduce lesser-known titles before pursuing distribution and streaming partnerships.

“We want audiences to discover Taiwan cinema beyond Taiwan New Cinema and see the many different facets of Taiwan,” TFAI tells Variety .

TFAI will also pitch its ongoing restoration of Yao Feng-pan’s “All in the Dim Cold Night” (1974) at MIFC’s Re>birth program on Oct. 15, seeking distributors and festival slots for the horror film. Often called Taiwan’s “King of Horror,” Yao built the film’s eerie atmosphere without modern visual effects, relying on practical techniques such as low-angle green lighting and burning straw on location.

Taiwan in Focus also includes a round table with TFAI chair Arthur Chu and programmer Howard Yang, a networking event and an exhibition of original Taiwanese film posters.

The institute hopes to build longer-term programming partnerships with international archives, giving restored Taiwanese films a life beyond their festival premieres. For “Osmanthus Alley,” the next step is securing overseas releases following its return to the screen.

article_text:
楽園追放 心のレゾナンス

劇場公開日： 2026年11月13日

解説・あらすじ

「機動戦士ガンダム00」シリーズの水島精二監督と「魔法少女まどか☆マギカ」などの脚本家・虚淵玄がタッグを組み、人類が電脳世界で暮らすようになった西暦2400年を舞台に繰り広げられる物語を描いた2014年の劇場用長編アニメ「楽園追放 Expelled from Paradise」の続編。 人類の多くが地上を捨て、データとなって電脳世界ディーヴァで暮らす西暦2400年。フロンティアセッターによるハッキングを発端に、ディーヴァの捜査官アンジェラ・バルザックの反逆が起こった。アンジェラにハッキングされ地上へと脱走した保安局のエージェントたちは、生身の体・マテリアルボディと共に、パーソナルデータを収納するハードウェアを強奪。その存在を地上に潜めた彼らは「フォールン」と名付けられ、ディーヴァへの脅威と化した。ディーヴァから捜索命令を受けた保安局エージェントのガブリエルたちは、フォールンとその謎にたどり着くべく奔走する。 スタッフ陣には水島精二監督をはじめ、脚本の虚淵玄、キャラクターデザインの齋藤将嗣、音楽のNARASAKIら前作のメンバーが再結集した。

article_text:
T his fierce film from socialist film-makers Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood gives us the story and the context of the Bradford 12. Twelve south Asian members of the United Black Youth League in 1981 were arrested on a charge of conspiracy to cause explosions for possessing dozens of molotov cocktails – milk bottles filled with petrol, with a rag through the lid – allegedly for throwing at the police. To the intense irritation of the British authorities, a mixed-race jury acquitted them, accepting their argument that it was in self-defence (and that the items themselves were closer to fireworks than bombs), because black and Asian communities were routinely and systematically attacked by skinheads and racists whose activities were shrugged at by the powers that be.

It is a reminder of a particularly ugly, squalid, bigoted and mediocre era in British public life, when Margaret Thatcher, just before becoming prime minister, tried to siphon off some of the far-right National Front’s political energy by declaring that people felt “swamped” by immigrants, the most earsplittingly loud dog whistle in Tory history. It was also the era when anti-racist protester Blair Peach was killed by the Met’s yet-to-be-disbanded special patrol group, when the still-unsolved New Cross fire in London took the lives of 13 young black people, when the south Asian woman Anwar Ditta was subject to a spitefully obstructive move from the Home Office to prevent her bringing her children into the UK – supposedly because they weren’t really hers, though a DNA test finally proved her right. Perhaps most of all, it was an era when the witness-box testimony of uniformed police officers was increasingly seen as almost valueless in these cases; the film also reminds us how culpably lackadaisical and incompetent the Yorkshire police were in catching the serial killer Peter Sutcliffe.

Rebellion is concerned with giving us a larger picture of liberationist politics, citing Frantz Fanon and bringing in Palestinian, South African, African American and Northern Irish voices. Here, however, I have one criticism: it is a shame, given the avowed importance of solidarity, that no interviewee can find it in their heart to say the word “antisemitism” – especially as the film uses a good deal of footage of the National Front, which had very open opinions about, and regularly attacked, Jews. It is clear that racism was something that was in the air then, along with casual misogyny and contempt for working people. Perhaps people conceal it better these days, but it’s still a shock to remember the sheer heavy weather of prejudice in those days, and to be reminded of those who stood up against it in court.

article_text:
Artículos

Estrenos Amazon Prime Video – 9 al 15 de noviembre 2026 y todo el mes

Staff Cine PREMIERE

¿Qué verás este mes?

Conoce aquí los estrenos de películas y series que llegan a la plataforma Amazon Prime Video México , en noviembre de 2026. Entre series originales, capítulos nuevos, temporadas que hacen su debut y películas que podrás disfrutar desde tu casa, los estrenos de Amazon Prime Video este mes se perfilan para ofrecer mucho entretenimiento.

Encuentra los estreno de películas y series en Amazon Prime Video de esta semana destacados en amarillo.

¿Cuál es el costo de Prime Video?

Después del periodo de prueba de 30 días, Amazon Prime Video cuesta $99 pesos al mes en México , mientras que el plan anual tiene un costo de $899 pesos . Asimismo, disfrutas del resto de los beneficios de Amazon, como envíos gratis en 1 o 2 días a nivel nacional.

Ahora, que si lo que quieres es tener acceso al catálogo sin anuncios comerciales, tendrás que pagar $50 pesos adicionales. Conoce más detalles de Amazon Prime Video .

Asimismo, a través del catálogo de Amazon Prime Video también te puedes suscribir a las siguientes plataformas sin salir del servicio de Prime: HBO Max, Paramount Plus, ViX Premium, Crunchyroll, MGM Plus, MUBI, Looke, Adrenalina Pura, Sony One o Fox Sports, entre otros.

También te podría interesar los estrenos de:

Películas de estreno en Amazon Prime Video, noviembre 2026

Insecta (Dir. Martín Florio, 2026) (12/11/2026)

La Mangosta (The Mongoose, Dir. Mark Vanselow) (4/11/2026) Ryan »Fang» Flanagan, un veterano de combate con numerosas condecoraciones, huye de la escena de un asesinato a 209 kilómetros por hora (130 millas por hora) en un Mustang Shelby Super Snake GT350.

Insecta (Dir. Martín Florio, 2026) (12/11/2026) ESTRENO ESTA SEMANA EN AMAZON PRIME VIDEO Protagonizada por Luis Felipe Tovar y Mayra Hermosillo, Insecta relata la historia de una famosa escritora de novelas de terror que regresa a una finca aislada para despedirse de su padre moribundo. Durante su estancia, comienza a sospechar que el monstruoso insecto que la atormentaba de niña podría ser más real de lo que pensaba.

Series de estreno en Amazon Prime Video, noviembre 2026

Blade Runner 2099 (25/11/2026)

El Señor de los Anillos: Los Anillos de Poder – temporada 3 (The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power) (4/11/2026) La temporada 3 tiene lugar en el apogeo de la Guerra de los Elfos y Sauron, mientras el Señor Oscuro busca forjar el Anillo Único que le dará la ventaja que necesita para ganar la guerra, atar a todos los pueblos a su voluntad y al fin gobernar toda la Tierra Media.

Blade Runner 2099 (25/11/2026) 50 años después de Blade Runner 2049, Cora, una fugitiva que busca dejar atrás su pasado, asume la identidad de una Blade Runner. Junto a Olwen, una replicante al borde de la muerte, deberá encontrar a un fugitivo que oculta un secreto capaz de destruir su ciudad.

article_text:
The only individual ever actually charged in the fatal 1996 shooting of Tupac Shakur was sentenced Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison.

Convicted of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon on August 31, Duane “Keff D” Davis was in court in Las Vegas today to learn his fate from Judge Carli Kierny.

Related Stories

Sky, Propagate & Passion Going Inside Tupac Shakur Trial

All Eyez On Guilty: Tupac Trial Jury Reaches Verdict In ‘Poetic Justice’ Star’s 1996 Drive-By Shooting Death

“You don’t get to take a man from his family,” the judge told Davis in announcing his sentence. Acknowledging how long it has taken for justice to be served in the death of the hip hop icon, she added: “You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future, from him… especially when that man is Tupac Shakur.”

Even with his bragging of involvement in Shakur’s murder in his memoir Compton Street Legend , to the cops, on TV and elsewhere over the years, Davis has insisted since his 2023 arrest that he was not guilty. In fact, the ex-gang leader has said he wasn’t even in Sin City that September night more than 30 years ago. Prosecutors claimed Davis acted out of revenge for Shakur and his crew previously beating on Orlando Anderson, Davis’ nephew.

Watch on Deadline

As he did when found guilty earlier this year, Davis today said, “I’m appealing this case for sure.”

In the aftermath of a September 7, 1996 Mike Tyson fight at Vegas’ MGM Grand, and at the height of the West Coast/East Coast rap beef, Shakur was shot by two rounds in the chest, one in the arm and one in the thigh, while in a car. Death Row Records boss Suge Knight was in a black BMW with Shakur when a mysterious a white Cadillac appeared and gunfire began. Knight lived, but the son of Black Panther activist Afeni Shakur died at the hospital six days later.

Like the subsequent death of Christopher “ Notorious B.I.G. ” Wallace in March 1997, what happened to Shakur and who was responsible for his demise remained an open case. Over the decades, as Shakur’s stature grew and evolved, there were flare-ups of media interest and theories but no conclusions or arrests.

The arrest and trial this year of Davis seemed to have ended a lot of that speculation.

Although Davis earlier in the hearing disputed not being allowed time served due to an incident with another inmate, he was silent today when Kierny delivered his sentence.

Before that, Tupac’s sister Sekyiwa Shakur addressed the court Tuesday on the personal and cultural loss resulting from the ‘California Love’ rapper’s death. Through Shakur’s remarks, Davis was seen rolling his eyes and making other reactions to her words. The Shakur sister asked Judge Kierny to give Davis the maximum time possible behind bars. It was a request reiterated in the Nevada courtroom by Shakur’s stepbrother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur too.

Already a legend by the time of his death and a movie star to boot, Shakur has been the posthumous subject of the likes of USA Network’s 2018 series Unsolved: The Murders of Tupac and Biggie Smalls , the 2017 doc Who Shot Biggie and Tupac? , the 2017 biopic All Eyez on Me from Summit, Morgan Creek, Program Pictures and Codeblack Films over the years.

Like the endless stream of remixes and unreleased tracks, there was also Nick Broomfield ’s 2002 feature-length documentary Biggie & Tupac ; FX’s Emmy-nominated series Dear Mama: The Saga of Afeni and Tupac Shakur , which premiered in 2023; and the Oscar-nominated 2003 film Tupac: Resurrection .

Dead at 25, Tupac would have been 55 if he were alive today.

article_text:
The Oscars will keep honoring human-driven work as AI spreads through filmmaking, Academy president Lynette Howell Taylor tells Variety in Tokyo, while the Academy’s leadership expects to keep refining the international feature rules in the first year of a new route that lets festivals qualify films.

Howell Taylor, Academy CEO Bill Kramer , chief membership, impact and industry officer Meredith Shea and Amy Homma, director and president of the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and Academy Collection, are in Japan for the Tokyo International Film Festival to meet members and filmmakers.

Related Stories

‘Bridgerton’ Spinoff, Centered on Lady Violet, Ordered by Netflix

'Bridgerton' Breakout Hannah Dodd to Lead Lucas Jones' Romantic Drama 'Miss You Forever, Zara Drake' (EXCLUSIVE)

Howell Taylor says AI has been part of post-production workflows for a decade and is already built into visual effects, and that the Academy discusses it regularly in relation to eligibility. “What will always remain true for the Academy is that we award human excellence, human-driven workflow,” she says. “And so, even though there’s a lot of exciting advances that can enhance the audience’s experience through technology, at the center of it will always be humans driving that workflow.” She also flags “very real concerns around copyright and around transparency and disclosure” as factors in the Academy’s thinking.

Under rules introduced for the 99th Oscars, a non-English-language film can now qualify for international feature without being its country’s official submission by winning the top prize at one of six festivals: the Golden Bear at Berlin, the Busan Award for best film, the Palme d’Or at Cannes, the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize at Sundance, the Platform Award at Toronto and the Golden Lion at Venice.

Asked whether eligibility could extend beyond the top prize at qualifying festivals, given that Andrey Zvyagintsev’s “Minotaur” nearly missed out after winning the Grand Prix rather than the Palme d’Or at Cannes, before France selected it as its submission, Shea says: “Each year, the International Feature Executive Committee will review the rules to ensure that they match industry standards. We were so proud this year to have the six festivals and the six highest honors from major international film festivals, and the committee will look at the rules to see how they need to make improvements and different edits just to ensure that it represents global filmmakers.”

Shea notes that festival qualification is not new for the Academy. The three shorts categories – animated, documentary and live action – already use qualifying festivals, as does documentary feature. The initial six festivals for international feature were picked according to their submission numbers and their reach around the world.

“I think it’s important to think about a couple of changes that have been made over the last couple of years. One was our rule to allow refugee filmmakers who are no longer in their home country to be represented by a country where they’re seeking asylum. And now we’ve added these six festival awards,” says Kramer. “All of this is designed to expand the aperture of how we’re inviting in non-U.S. films, non-English-language films, to be considered for the International Feature Film Award. So, we are always looking at ways to invite more filmmakers into that mix. So, this is part of that, and I think you will see that continue.”

Howell Taylor says the refugee rule and the festival route were both designed in part to help filmmakers working in exile, whose governments would be unlikely to put their films forward, so that “there are now multiple paths to qualify for an international award rather than just being selected by a home country.”

Shea says international feature is one category, and that films can also be submitted for documentary feature, animated feature and Best Picture. “I think it’s important for global filmmakers to know that those categories and Best Picture are open to all filmmakers,” she says. Howell Taylor adds that last year’s Oscars had international representation in every category.

The Tokyo visit forms part of a wider push. “This is all part of our globalization efforts,” Kramer says. “The Academy, just like the film industry, is becoming more global in scope and scale. From our museum exhibitions and programs to our membership – we’re now 25% non-U.S. membership – you’re seeing it in our nominations and awards. So, we are out in the world meeting with our members and filmmakers.”

The Academy has been to Rio, Marrakesh and Morelia, with team members also attending Busan. Kramer says he is “thrilled to be at the Tokyo International Film Festival,” adding: “We’re having an incredible time. Very impressive.”

For Shea, festival partners such as Tokyo give the Academy a foothold in each region. “It’s so important for us as an organization to go where our members are,” she says. “There’s a built-in film audience, so that includes members, individuals that are looking to become Academy members, and emerging filmmakers that want to engage with our global talent development programs.”

Shea says the Academy uses the international feature category to find new members, since the films arriving from around the world bring filmmakers who already clear a bar of excellence in their own countries. Using the category to identify new members across all disciplines “has been wildly successful for us, and that’s why you’ve seen our invitees over the last five years be increasingly global,” she says.

Smaller film industries in South and Southeast Asia face a separate hurdle: the cost of awards campaigns. “Talent is universal, but accessibility is not always the same for everybody,” says Howell Taylor. “Our role as an Academy is to travel to where the filmmaking communities are, meet filmmakers, have conversations about barriers to entry. … As an Academy, we’re not in charge of awards spending, but we continue to have deep conversations with filmmakers around the world, and especially in the smaller regions, on what is it that would help them with their own barriers to entry and how can we support.”

Kramer cites the Academy Screening Room, the organization’s streaming service for members, where every film is presented on equal terms. Voters must also agree, on an honor system, to watch every film in a category before casting a ballot, while the Academy spotlights emerging, diverse and international filmmakers on its social channels and in the museum. “So, we work very hard to level that playing field because there are different ways of campaigning, and ultimately we want our members to vote for excellence. That’s what’s key,” he says.

Members, Kramer adds, “are curious. They love movies, so they will seek out those films. We just have to make them aware of them, and that’s our job.”

Planning has already begun for the 2029 ceremony, the first under the Academy’s deal with YouTube. “The goal of moving the show to YouTube was to reach a larger global audience,” Kramer says. “YouTube has the potential of reaching 2.5 billion people around the world. They will see the same Oscars show at the same time and have the option of watching it in over 30 languages. That was very important to us as we think about our global expansion.”

Kramer says the show’s non-U.S. audience is already roughly equal to its U.S. audience. “There’s a great demand for the Oscars outside of the U.S., and YouTube will help us reach a much larger international audience. And it allows us to engage with our fans more directly. So, we have much more control over the fan engagement and the audience engagement,” he says.

On whether the ceremony’s start time could shift to suit viewers in other regions, he says: “We’re looking at a lot of things right now, to be determined.”

Asked about a more permanent presence in Asia, Kramer says: “I think you will see a continuation of our travel around the world to meet our members and filmmakers where they live and work. We do have many more options now to engage with our members and the filmmaking public.”

He notes that a London office coordinates many of the Academy’s non-U.S. initiatives, that the museum’s screening series now travels to New York and London, and that the Academy has more than 200 partnerships with writing labs, universities and film schools worldwide through its talent development programs and the museum. “You’ll only see an expansion of that,” he says.

Howell Taylor says the Academy is “always evolving” and that “there’s a lot of stuff that’s on the table.” Shea adds that the Student Academy Awards, the Nicholl Fellowship in screenwriting and the Gold Fellowship for Women, run in partnership with Chanel, have seen an increase in international winners.

At the Academy Museum, which opened in 2021 and runs roughly 600 repertory screenings a year alongside exhibitions across four floors, Homma says the brief extends well beyond North American film history. “We look forward to continuing to build on the momentum and success we’ve already seen in featuring more Asian and Asian American film histories and stories,” she says.

On film preservation, a pressing issue across Asia, Homma says the work of archives and collecting institutions has never been more critical if more films are not to be lost or left unrestored. The museum’s annual Present Past series screens restoration premieres from the Academy and the wider archival community. “I think it’s imperative that we all link arms as an archival community right now, to not only do this work of preservation, but to also build the audience for it, and to build the understanding of what will happen if we don’t take these efforts,” Homma says.

With the Academy’s centennial approaching, Howell Taylor says reaching 100 years is a chance to reflect on how the film industry has changed in the U.S. and abroad, with the Academy creating content over the next 18 months in the run-up.

“You will continue to see growth in our international membership. You will continue to see international programming in our museum. You will continue to see our Academy Collection growing international representation within the collection,” says Kramer. “So, we’re moving in a very exciting global direction, and that will continue.”
